90% of people: "What's UX/UI?"

Me: "It's basically app and web design on steroids."

This is the generic answer I give to anyone who has never heard of UX/UI or product design before. It's a lot easier and quicker than explaining what UX/UI actually is, because the real explanation can be a bit of a mouthful. So this time I thought I'd actually show what I do, by taking one real world case study from start to finish.

UX/UI (and the many, many job titles that come with it) is fixing real problems that businesses and users have, while making the product as simple and easy to use as possible. Maybe that isn't such a mouthful after all. Sometimes the problem is small, like a home button that takes you to settings, or yellow text on a white background that nobody can read, and designers are there to catch those before they ever reach a customer. Every now and then, though, a designer gets to solve a problem that hardly anyone realised existed, and this case study is about one of those.

It started in a Dutch Lidl

I was recently on holiday in the Netherlands and found myself in a Lidl (I like to treat myself when I go abroad). In a lot of Dutch supermarkets you can't just walk out with your shopping. You have to scan a barcode to open the exit gates, which I assume is there to put off shoplifters. Scanning a receipt to get through a barrier isn't new in the UK either, and it isn't limited to supermarkets. Morrisons and Sainsbury's have exit barriers in some stores, and so does Primark.

What impressed me was that my friend didn't need a slip of paper to get out, because the barcode was sitting in the supermarket's loyalty app on his phone. That got me thinking. If the gate barcode can live on your phone, why can't the receipt? And come to think of it, why are most of us in the UK still being handed a curl of paper at the till in 2026? The question stuck with me, so I started digging into what moving supermarket receipts onto a loyalty app could do for the shop, the shopper and everyone in between.

The receipt problem, in numbers

Before the maths

Nobody publishes an exact count of the receipts printed in the UK each year. What follows combines the best data I could find with a few clearly labelled assumptions, and all the working is at the end so you can check it.

The figure you'll see quoted most often is that the UK prints roughly 11.2 billion receipts a year, which comes from industry research published by Retail Voices in 2022. Even that number has a slightly mysterious past. While researching, I found a trade article from well over a decade ago quoting the very same 11.2 billion, except it described them as Tesco's receipts alone, so it's best treated as a ballpark rather than gospel. Taking it at face value, the Beat The Receipt campaign estimates that those receipts cost around £32 million a year to produce (a little more than Manchester United paid Spurs for Dimitar Berbatov in 2008), use up around 200,000 trees and consume 1.6 billion litres of water.

You might also see these figures paired with 680,000 tonnes of paper waste and a carbon footprint equal to 400,000 cars. I've deliberately left both out. Divide 680,000 tonnes by 11.2 billion and every single receipt would weigh around 60 grams, roughly the same as a medium egg, when a real till receipt weighs a gram or two.

So how many of those receipts come from supermarkets? Kantar, one of the world's biggest market research firms and the industry standard for UK grocery data, counted 490 million trips to UK supermarkets in the four weeks to 15 June 2025. There are thirteen of those four week periods in a year, so 490 million × 13 gives us around 6.37 billion supermarket trips a year. One month in June won't capture the Christmas rush or a quiet January, so think of this as a reasonable estimate rather than an exact count.

Not every trip ends with a printed receipt, though. Most supermarket shopping now goes through self-checkouts, which ask whether you want one, and plenty of us tap "no", especially for a quick top-up shop. Nobody publishes how often that happens in the UK, so I've assumed around 30% of supermarket receipts are already declined. It's a judgement call rather than a measured figure, and the working at the end shows how the numbers change at 20% and 50%. That leaves roughly 4.46 billion printed supermarket receipts a year (6.37 billion × 0.7), or about 40% of every receipt printed in the UK.

Who actually loses out?

Once you look closely, the problem turns out to have a few layers, and it touches pretty much everyone involved.

The business

Retailers spend millions every year printing something most of us bin within minutes, or never pick up at all.

The planet

Trees, water and energy all go into a slip of paper hardly anyone reads, and shiny thermal receipt paper often can't go in the recycling.

The customer

The classic "I've lost the receipt" moment when something needs returning, or the receipt has faded to a blank strip by the time you need it.

The staff

Cashiers handle hundreds of receipts a day. Thermal paper is coated in chemical developers, and while the EU restricted BPA in receipts in 2020, scientists are still studying some of the chemicals that replaced it.

So what about Tesco?

The UK's biggest supermarket chain is Tesco, with 27.9% of the grocery market according to Kantar. That figure is a share of what people spend rather than how many trips they make, so applying it to receipts is an assumption, but it gets us close enough. More quick maths: 4.46 billion × 0.279 gives us roughly 1.24 billion Tesco receipts a year. That's about 11% of every receipt printed in the UK, so I've scaled the UK figures down by the same amount.

This isn't me having a pop at Tesco (they make a great sourdough loaf and sell very good beef sausages). It's me gathering evidence that digital receipts could make a genuine difference for the retailer, its customers, its staff and the environment, and Tesco happens to be the best place to prove it.

Hang on, doesn't this already exist?

Here's the twist, and I only found it because I went looking for competitors, which is exactly what a designer should do before drawing a single screen. Remember that Lidl in the Netherlands? Lidl's Plus app has offered digital receipts in the UK since it launched in 2020. You scan the app at the till and the receipt appears on your phone.

Tesco has even tried it before. In 2016 it trialled paperless receipts at the self-service tills of two stores in Harlow, using a separate app, and said at the time that a future version could connect to Clubcard. As far as I can tell, it never made it past the trial.

Today, the Tesco app does give you digital receipts, but only for online orders. For shopping in store, the Clubcard app keeps a basic transaction history: the date, the store, how much you spent and the points you earned. What it doesn't show is what you actually bought.

Of the UK's biggest supermarkets, Lidl is the only one I could find that saves itemised receipts for in-store shopping. Apps change often, though, so this is based on public information as of October 2026.

So the idea isn't new, and that's actually good news. Lidl has already shown that customers will use it, and Tesco already holds most of the data it needs, because every in-store shop is recorded against your Clubcard anyway. The real question is no longer whether this could work. It's why the UK's biggest supermarket hasn't done it yet, and how it should be designed when it does.

Why Tesco would care

Let's be honest about the money first. £3.5 million a year sounds like a lot, but for a business the size of Tesco it's small change, so paper savings alone won't win anyone over in a boardroom. The stronger case is everything that comes with it.

Clubcard is already used in around 80% of Tesco transactions, according to the company's chief customer officer, so most receipts are flowing through Clubcard already. Giving people a reason to open the app after a shop, not just before it, is valuable to any retailer. Searchable receipts mean fewer "I've lost my receipt" conversations at the customer service desk. And a measurable cut in paper is something Tesco can point to in its sustainability reporting.

The audience is already there, too. As of 2024, 23 million of the UK's 28.3 million households have a Clubcard, and 12.7 million people use the Clubcard app. That's at least 12.7 million customers who could have their receipts land in the app from day one.

So how would you actually design it?

Excellent question, so let's imagine I actually work for Tesco, or any leading UK supermarket for that matter. After doing the research above, I'd present it to stakeholders, including the teams I'd normally work alongside, like development and marketing, because they'd all have a part to play. A product owner or director would usually write up the timelines and the full project brief. Once I got the go ahead, the next steps would be talking to real customers, then creating user personas, a user journey map and low fidelity designs, usually in that order.

For this concept I haven't been able to interview Tesco customers, so the personas below are what designers call proto-personas. They're educated guesses based on desk research, and on a real project they'd be tested and refined through interviews and surveys before anyone relied on them.

Who are we designing for?

A user persona is a made up customer who represents a real group of people using the product. We create them so we can empathise with those users and understand what they actually need, because if we design with them in mind, we cover as many real customers as possible. A video streaming service, for example, might have one persona on a tight budget who happily sits through adverts to pay less, and another who can't stand adverts and will pay more to avoid them. For digital receipts, there are four main types of customer.

P

Priya, 29

Has a Clubcard and uses the app
"I kept the receipt for my toaster for months, then binned it the week before it broke."
Situation
Does a big weekly shop and grabs bits from her local Express, scanning the app every time.
Goal
Keep track of what she spends and never lose a receipt again.
What changes
Every receipt lands in the app automatically, searchable by store or product.
D

Dave, 54

Doesn't have a Clubcard
"I just want to pay and get out. I don't need another card or another app."
Situation
Pays by card and takes a paper receipt when he thinks he might need it.
Goal
A quick, simple shop with nothing to sign up for.
What changes
Nothing at all. His till experience stays exactly the same, paper receipt included.
T

Tom, 41

Has a Clubcard but not the app
"The card in my wallet works fine, so I've never seen the point of the app."
Situation
Scans a plastic Clubcard for the points and prices, and has never downloaded the app.
Goal
Get the Clubcard prices without any extra effort.
What changes
His receipts are saved to his Clubcard account anyway, ready in the app or on tesco.com whenever he wants them.
M

Maureen, 72

Has a Clubcard, no smartphone
"The print on my receipts fades so quickly I can never read them when I need to."
Situation
Keeps her Clubcard on her keyring and uses a laptop at home.
Goal
Check her shopping and keep proof of purchase for anything expensive.
What changes
She can view and print any receipt from her Tesco account on her laptop.

What changes at the till? Almost nothing

So how do we design the new feature with all four of these customers in mind? That turns out to be easier than you might think. This project only adds the ability to get receipts onto Clubcard, viewable in the app or on the website. It doesn't take anything away, so the journey at the till stays the same for every persona.

Every customer scans their shopping, scans their Clubcard if they have one, takes a receipt or doesn't, and leaves. The only difference in the new journey is that if they scanned their Clubcard, the receipt is already waiting for them in the app. There's no new setting to switch on and no extra question at the till, because self-checkouts already ask whether you want a receipt printed. That's deliberate, because the best kind of feature is one customers get without having to learn anything new, and once people know their receipt is safe in the app, more of them will simply tap "no receipt".

Sketching it out

After the personas and the journey map, it's time for low fidelity designs. These can be pen and paper sketches, or slightly tidier wireframes in a tool like Balsamiq or Canva. The point is to work out where things go before worrying about how they look.

The biggest decision at this stage was where receipts should live. The Tesco app has five tabs along the bottom (Home, Favourites, Search, Clubcard and Baskets), and adding a sixth would squeeze every tab and make them all harder to tap. Receipts belong to your Clubcard anyway, so the feature sits inside the Clubcard tab as a new card.

The high fidelity prototype

Normally I'd build the high fidelity version in Figma, using the company's design system and component library (hopefully they'd have one). For this case study I've built it as a working prototype instead, styled on the real Tesco app, so you can click through it right here.

Things to try

  • Tap Clubcard, then the green Receipts card
  • Search for "oat milk" to see which shops it was in
  • Sort by highest spend, or filter to one store
  • Open a receipt, then try "Show in-store"
  • Remove a receipt, then undo it

Inside Clubcard, not a new tab

Receipts sit as the first card in the Clubcard tab, with a small "New" badge, so the bottom navigation stays exactly as customers know it.

Launched through a banner people already see

The home screen already has a promotional banner slot, so that's where the feature is announced, rather than in a pop up that gets in the way.

Search inside receipts, not just stores

"When did I last buy oat milk?" is a question a paper receipt can never answer, so search looks through every item as well as store names.

Sort and filter in one place

Sort by date or spend and filter by store or date range in one sheet, with active filters shown as chips you can tap to remove.

Remove, with a safety net

Clubcard accounts are often shared within a household, so you can remove a receipt from your list (handy for hiding a surprise present). There's a confirmation step and an undo, and Tesco still keeps the record for points and returns.

"Show in-store" instead of "Start a return"

My first version had a "Start a return" button, but nobody returns a pint of milk through an app. Grocery returns happen at the desk, so the button now brings up a barcode a colleague can scan as proof of purchase.

Accessible by default

WCAG AA colour contrast, 44px tap targets, an 8pt spacing grid, labels for screen readers and visible focus states throughout.

And for customers without a smartphone

Maureen doesn't have a smartphone, but she does have a laptop. The same receipts appear in her Tesco account on tesco.com, with the same search and filters, and a print button for anything she wants on paper.

How I'd test it, and how we'd know it worked

Once a prototype exists, the next step is putting it in front of real people. A first round can be as simple as five people working through a few tasks while you watch: find the receipt for last Saturday's shop, find out when you last bought oat milk, and show a receipt at the customer service desk. Watching where people hesitate will tell you more than any amount of guessing, and every change it leads to goes back into the design.

If the feature launched, I'd judge it on a handful of numbers: the share of Clubcard shops where the customer chooses not to print a receipt, how often people open their receipts, how many "lost receipt" conversations happen at customer service desks, and how many paper till rolls each store orders.

Presenting to stakeholders

When the high fidelity prototype is ready, it's time to present your banging new designs to your own team first. The feedback will be one of two things: positive reinforcement that you are in fact good at your job, or helpful tips, and both are useful. Once you've made any changes, and possibly shown the team again, it's time to present to the stakeholders. That usually means a PowerPoint, so it's time to wind back to secondary school IT and dust off those presentation skills.

What could it actually save?

If Tesco rolled this out through the Clubcard app, nobody would stop printing receipts overnight. Adoption would build as more people discover the feature and get comfortable skipping the paper copy. To estimate how quickly, I built a simple model from three real starting points, and capped it so it can't promise the impossible.

80%

Only Clubcard shops count

Clubcard is used in around 80% of Tesco transactions. The other 20% will always get paper.

55% → 70%

Not every Clubcard shop uses the app

About 55% of Clubcard households have the app today (12.7m of 23m). I've grown that by 5% a year, much slower than Clubcard's own growth, because Clubcard already reaches 81% of UK households.

40% → 79%

Not everyone skips paper straight away

The share of app users who stop printing rises each year to 79%, from a 2025 Yocuda survey of loyalty card members. Yocuda sells digital receipts, so take it with a pinch of salt.

In Year 1, with the feature still bedding in, I estimate nearly one in five of Tesco's paper receipts would no longer be printed, saving around £660,000 and 4,122 trees. By Year 3 that rises to a third of all receipts, saving £1.18 million and 7,384 trees. By Year 5, close to half of Tesco's receipts would go unprinted, saving around £1.58 million and 9,894 trees in that single year. Add it all up across the first five years and the total comes to roughly 2 billion receipts, £5.75 million, 35,939 trees and 288 million litres of water, all from changing how a receipt gets to the customer.

These numbers are smaller than the ones I first came up with, and that's on purpose. My first model assumed almost every Tesco shopper would end up using the app, which quietly ignored everyone without a Clubcard or a smartphone, and grew Clubcard so fast it would have had more members than there are households in the UK. A smaller number you can defend is worth far more than a big one that falls apart, and none of this is a Tesco forecast. It's a scenario built from public data.

What if every supermarket did it?

Tesco is only one supermarket, and almost every big UK supermarket already runs a loyalty scheme with an app, from Sainsbury's Nectar and Asda Rewards to Morrisons More, Co-op Membership and Lidl Plus. The notable exception is Aldi, which has made not having a loyalty scheme part of its advertising. Between them, the supermarkets with apps account for more than three quarters of all UK grocery spending.

UK supermarkets as a whole print around 4.46 billion receipts a year, even after the ones people already decline, costing roughly £12.7 million and using around 80,000 trees and 637 million litres of water. If every supermarket with an app reached the level I've estimated for Tesco by Year 5, around 1.5 billion supermarket receipts a year would never be printed.

That's very much a best case, because Tesco's Clubcard is unusually popular, and for comparison, the Lidl Plus app is used by around 38% of shoppers. But it shows what happens when one good idea becomes the norm across a whole industry, rather than a feature one supermarket happens to have.

What this can't fix

Would this get rid of paper receipts in UK supermarkets completely? To put it simply, no, because not every customer has a loyalty card, not everyone has a smartphone or a computer, and some people simply prefer paper, which is completely fine. Digital receipts aren't entirely free of impact either, because storing them uses servers and energy, although a few kilobytes of data per shop is far lighter than a strip of thermal paper. And every number in this case study is an estimate built on public data and stated assumptions rather than Tesco's own figures. If I were doing this inside Tesco, my first job would be swapping my assumptions for their real data.

So, what is UX/UI?

Remember the question I started with? Here's the longer answer. A receipt is about as boring as everyday objects get, but behind it sits a problem that costs money, uses up trees and water, frustrates customers and has a genuinely simple fix. UX/UI is spotting a problem like that, checking whether it's real, understanding who it affects, and designing a fix so simple that most people barely notice it happening. You scan your Clubcard like you always do, and the receipt is just there.

UX/UI is fixing a real problem that users and businesses have, while making the product as simple and easy to use as possible.

So the next time someone asks what I do, I'll probably still say "app and web design on steroids". The only difference is that now, when they look confused, I can just send them this.

How the numbers work

Supermarket receipts. Kantar counted 490 million UK supermarket trips in the four weeks to 15 June 2025. 490m × 13 four week periods = 6.37bn trips a year. Assuming around 30% of trips end without a printed receipt, 6.37bn × 0.7 = 4.46bn printed receipts, which is 39.8% of the 11.2bn UK total.

Declined receipts. There's no published UK figure for how often shoppers decline a receipt. Around 80% of sales in a typical supermarket now go through self-checkouts, which ask before printing (The Grocer). A US YouGov survey found 8% of people skip receipts altogether, rising to 17% of 18 to 24 year olds, and estimates of the impact of France's receipt-on-request law assume a 20% drop in printed receipts. The 30% used here is my own judgement based on those. At 20% the five year Tesco saving would be about £6.57m, and at 50% about £4.11m.

Tesco receipts. 4.46bn × 27.9% (Tesco's Kantar grocery market share, a share of spending rather than trips) = 1.24bn a year, which is 11.1% of the 11.2bn UK total.

Tesco's footprint. The UK totals (£32m, 200,000 trees, 1.6bn litres of water) × 11.1% = £3.55m, 22,215 trees and 178m litres. This assumes an average Tesco receipt uses the same resources as any other receipt.

Left out on purpose. The widely quoted 680,000 tonnes of paper works out at about 60g per receipt, and the 400,000 cars figure can't be traced to a clear method, so neither is used here.

The five year model. Share of Tesco receipts not printed = 80% (Clubcard transactions) × app share of Clubcard shops × share of app users who skip paper. App share starts at 55% (12.7m app users ÷ 23m Clubcard households) and grows 5% a year: 57.8%, 60.6%, 63.7%, 66.9%, 70.2%. The share who skip paper rises 40%, 55%, 65%, 72%, 79%. Savings = 1.24bn × that share, assuming app users currently print receipts as often as everyone else, with the cost, trees and water scaled per receipt.

Every supermarket. 4.46bn printed supermarket receipts × 77.3% (combined market share of Tesco, Sainsbury's, Asda, Lidl, Morrisons and Co-op) × Tesco's Year 5 rate of 44.5% = 1.54bn receipts a year.

Known weaknesses. The 11.2bn baseline is old and hard to trace. The 30% decline rate is an assumption rather than a measured figure. Different data sources come from different years (2022 to 2026).
